items.title: US economy roars ahead in third quarter, inflation remains high in October By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 25 (Reuters) - The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027. The sharp upward revision to gross domestic product last quarter, reported by the Commerce Department on Wednesday, marked the quickest economic growth pace in three years. It reflected upgrades to consumer spending and business investment, mostly related to artificial intelligence. Robust domestic demand is fueling inflation, with a measure of underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-over-year increase since late 2023. The economy has powered ahead despite the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran. "It is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "It was once thought that import tariffs and energy prices from the Mideast war were one-off factors behind the higher inflation numbers, but increasingly the inflation fires look to be stoked by old-fashioned economic demand pressures." GDP increased at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its second estimate of third-quarter GDP. It was the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2023. ... Growth in consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, was revised up to a 4.2% rate. That was the strongest pace since the fourth quarter of 2024 and was an upgrade from the previously reported 3.8% pace. Spending is being driven mostly by higher-income households, whose wealth was boosted by the stock market before the ongoing AI-led selloff. Economists expect consumer spending to slow to a still-healthy pace in the fourth quarter, though declining gasoline prices should ease some of the financial pressure on middle- and lower-income households. ... The Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index increased 0.3% in October after gaining 0.5% in September, the BEA said. PCE inflation was lifted by higher prices for goods, including food and household furnishings, as well as services such as recreation, dining out and hotel stays. In the 12 months through October, PCE inflation increased 3.8% after advancing 3.6% in September. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the PCE Price Index increased 0.3% for the third straight month. items.title: Fed survey shows continued economic growth, sticky inflation in recent weeks By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 25 (Reuters) - Economic growth persisted at a "slight to moderate" pace across most of the US in recent weeks, while inflation remained sticky and employment levels rose, a Federal Reserve survey showed on Wednesday, two weeks before central bank policymakers decide whether to raise interest rates. "Prices increased moderately overall, as in the prior reporting period," the Fed said in its latest "Beige Book" report, a compendium of survey-based data and commentary from businesses compiled by its 12 regional banks to provide a read on economic conditions. "Contacts across a range of sectors reported sustained cost pressure from energy, transportation, health care, insurance, and tariff-related expenses." Still, input costs were outpacing selling price increases, suggesting growing pressure on corporate margins, the report said. "(C)ompetitive pressures and customer price sensitivity limited firms’ ability to fully pass through higher costs. Contacts expected both expenses and prices to continue rising in the coming months."

items.title: GDP (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026 | U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
items.excerpt: EMBARGOED UNTIL RELEASE AT 8:30 a.m. EST, Wednesday, November 25, 2026 # GDP (Second Estimate) and Corporate Profits, 3rd Quarter 2026 Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 4.3 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the second estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent. The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. Real GDP was revised up 0.9 percentage point from the advance estimate, primarily reflecting upward revisions to investment and consumer spending. For more information, refer to the " Technical Notes" below. Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 5.8 percent in the third quarter, revised up 0.9 percentage point from the previous estimate. The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 2.7 percent in the third quarter, revised down 0.3 percentage point from the previous estimate. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, both the same as previously estimated. Real gross domestic income (GDI) increased 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent (revised) in the second quarter. The average of real GDP and real GDI also increased 4.4 percent, compared with an increase of 2.2 percent (revised).

items.excerpt: Trump Administration Proposes Tariffs on 14 Partners The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. The U.S. Trade Representative’s office said the duties respond to excess factory capacity abroad, Reuters reported, and would be capped at levels set in completed or pending trade deals. China would face a 20% rate that could rise to 40% if its trade truce with Washington falls apart. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs would not take effect until after a Jan. 25 public hearing. Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat expected to chair the Senate Finance Committee, said he would work to end them. 1, 2 Second Judge Blocks Trump Birthright Citizenship Order A second federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration’s latest effort to restrict birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Christopher R. Cooper of Washington, D.C., issued a preliminary injunction in a 67-page opinion, The Hill reported. The order prevents federal authorities from enforcing the president’s August executive orders, which sought to narrow who qualifies for citizenship at birth. Cooper wrote that the Supreme Court “has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law.” A federal judge in Maryland blocked the administration’s effort in September. 3 Judge Halts FCC Early Review of ABC Station Licenses A federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Federal Communications Commission from continuing an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses. In a 45-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan found that ABC is likely to succeed in showing the review was retaliatory, CBS News reported. Her preliminary injunction applies while the network’s lawsuit proceeds. The FCC earlier this year ordered ABC to file early renewal applications for its eight local stations. The agency has denied seeking to punish the network for its speech. An FCC spokesperson called the decision “wrong on the facts and wrong on the law.” 4 ... Judge Declines to Extend Ban on Pro-Trump Federal Ads A federal judge on Wednesday declined to extend a temporary ban on taxpayer-funded government ads that promoted President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan ruled against the Democratic National Committee, which sued in October and argued the ads were illegal propaganda, the Associated Press reported. AliKhan wrote that the midterm elections “have come and gone.” She also said the committee was likely to succeed on its claim that using public money for the ads violated the law. A committee spokesperson said the organization was disappointed. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements. 6 ... Meeks Urges Halt to Federal Role in Lukoil Purchase Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, on Wednesday called on the Trump administration to stop a proposed purchase of Lukoil’s international assets. In a statement released by the committee’s Democrats, Meeks said the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation and billionaire investors are involved in the proposed deal. He said Congress banned the agency from investing in Russia less than a year ago, and he put the value of the energy assets at $10 billion. Meeks said the agency exists to advance development in emerging markets. He added that Congress will continue to demand answers. ...
